text: It may be objected that the chapter merely reflects the economy of ancient narrative, which rarely reports what its characters feel and never explains it; and there is perhaps some truth in the objection. But the narrator of Genesis is not everywhere so sparing. The reticence of chapter 22 is deliberate, and in this narrator restraint becomes a kind of accusation. He knows what he is doing, for elsewhere he states plainly what his people feel: Esau cries out, Jacob is afraid, Joseph weeps.
